say: Good morning, Data Detectives! A graph is a picture of numbers. A good detective reads it carefully, and also checks whether the picture is telling the truth.
Today we read line graphs and tables, find numbers that are missing, and catch a graph that tries to trick us. Notice it. Test it. Explain why.
Here are four tiny graphs with no numbers at all. I will read a story. Point to the graph that tells the story, and be ready to say why.
Listen: a bath filling up with water. Which line? Why not the one that goes up and then down?
You will plot the queue at a chicken rice stall from 11:00 to 2:00. Before you plot: at what time do you think the queue is longest? Write your guess at the top of your grid.
stuck: Stuck on the scale: the biggest number is 22. If each line is 2 people, how many lines do you need to reach 22?
Points in the wrong place: put your finger on the time, go straight up, then check the number on the side.
Finished early: between which two times did the queue grow the most? Show it on your graph without working out every change.

say: “First the title and the axes: books borrowed, Monday to Friday. Then the scale: each line on the side is worth 10. Tuesday’s point is on the 40 line, so 40. Monday’s point is halfway between 20 and 30, so 25.”

“Which day had the biggest change? I list each change: Monday to Tuesday up 15, Tuesday to Wednesday down 5, Wednesday to Thursday up 25, Thursday to Friday down 10. The biggest increase is 25, and on the graph it is the steepest line going up.”
“A table with missing numbers: Ali’s row must add up to 61. 61 − 26 = 35. I fill the rows first, then the columns. Last, I check: the column totals and the row totals must give the same grand total.”

do: Point to a line and ask: “Is this an increase or a decrease? By how much?”
Ask: “What is each line on the side worth? How do you know?”
Ask: “How can you check your missing number?”
stuck: Hint 1: “Find what one line on the scale is worth before you read anything.”
Hint 2: “Write the change between each pair of neighbours, with up or down.”
Hint 3: “Add the numbers you know, then take them away from the total.”

say: “Two graphs show the same numbers, but one line looks much steeper. How can that be?”
“How would you draw a fair graph if you wanted to compare two shops?”
ask: “Two graphs show the same numbers, but one line looks much steeper. How can that be?”
The scales are different. If a scale starts at a big number, or each line is worth very little, a small change looks huge. To compare fairly, use the same scale for both graphs, starting at 0.

say: “Today you read graphs like detectives: scale first, then the changes, and you caught a graph that was trying to trick you.”
“Hand me your exit ticket and I will stamp your inquiry journal.”

p4l9-title.note: Objective: Read values and trends from line graphs (using the scale), find the biggest increase or decrease, find missing values in tables and graphs from totals and patterns, compare two lines on one graph, and explain why a graph with a different scale can mislead. Thinking strategies today: READ THE SCALE FIRST, LIST THE CHANGES, and WORK FROM THE TOTAL. Materials: Mini whiteboards, a ruler and two coloured pencils per child, printed blank graph grids (or squared paper), the queue table for the explore task. Online: children use a printed blank grid or squared paper and hold it up to the camera; the tutor plots on the slide graphs while children call out where each point goes. Time plan: opening 0 to 1, sneak-peek puzzles 1 to 4 (two ideas we have not learnt yet; answers shown to the tutor only, on camera, nobody marked), warm-up game 4 to 6 (one short round), quick questions 6 to 8, explore 8 to 18 (a Go further what-if is on the slide from minute 8), teaching 18 to 30 (click to reveal each step and answer; the "your turn" slides are optional, skip them if short of time), brain break 30 to 34, worksheet page 1 (Start here, in pairs) 34 to 50 and check together 50 to 53, short teaching before page 2 53 to 58, worksheet page 2 (on your own) 58 to 76 and check together 76 to 80, talk time 80 to 85, exit ticket 85 to 88, looking back (reflection) 88 to 90 (2 minutes). After question 3 every child may choose: carry on, or try the Think harder page. Think harder, Go further and the Investigation have no fixed time slot: any child may choose them at any time, or take them home. The tutor never announces who is on which page, and pairs are not split unless both children agree. Online: page 1 is pair work, so allow about 2 minutes to move into and out of breakout rooms (or run page 1 as a whole-group screen-share if there are only 8 children).

p4l9-check.note: Minutes 1 to 4 (3 minutes). SNEAK-PEEK PUZZLES. Say: "These are ideas we have not learnt yet. Guessing is welcome, drawing is welcome and so is saying I do not know. Nobody is marked, and nobody's answer is shown to the group." Puzzle 1 is a TRY IT puzzle: any child can start it with objects, a drawing or counting, so everyone has a first win. Puzzle 2 needs a little thinking. About 90 seconds each. Children show their answers PRIVATELY: written on their own paper and held to the camera at the same moment for everyone (or shown only to you on camera). Never use private chat or DMs. Never ask for boards up in front of the group, never read out whose answer is whose, and never say who got it right. Then click to show each answer and talk it through for everyone ("some of you tried ..."), naming no child. Ask for volunteers first if you want a reason said aloud; nobody is called on by name, and passing is always fine. ANSWERS: 1) Tuesday sold the most (45). Wednesday sold the fewest (25). 2) 125. Halfway between 100 and 150 is 100 + 25. A GOOD REASON: Read the scale first: what is each line worth? Halfway between two lines is half of the step. Use what you see only to plan your help. It does not decide who is on which page and it is not recorded as a mark. After question 3 on page 1 every child may choose: carry on, or try the Think harder page. Make the invitation to the WHOLE group ("when you have finished Start here you can choose Think harder, Go further or the Investigation"), so nobody is singled out. Never message a child privately, never name a child, and never announce who is on which page. Everyone stays in the same room and every child turns to the page they choose. If a pair would be split, ask both children first; never leave a child alone on page 1 (join them to another pair or to yourself).

p4l9-warm1.note: Minutes 4 to 6 (one short round, about 2 minutes: the Sneak-peek puzzles came first). Which graph tells the story? The graphs have no numbers on purpose: we read the SHAPE. Read story 1 aloud. Children point at (or write the letter of) the matching graph, then say why before you click. Clicks reveal the answers in order. Answers: 1) Graph C: the water goes up steadily. 2) Graph A: people arrive for lunch, then leave. 3) Graph D: the candle gets shorter steadily. 4) Graph B: nothing changes, so the line is flat. Ask: "Could the hawker centre graph be another shape on a rainy day?" "Make up a story for a line that goes DOWN, then UP." (e.g. water in a bathtub as it drains and is filled again). Listen for "steep" and "flat": we use those words all lesson.

p4l9-warm2.note: Minutes 6 to 8. Whiteboards up together, then click. Each one is a skill for today: 1) 27, the size of a change. 2) 45, reading halfway between two grid lines. 3) 100: add 85 + 15. 4) 45: 45 + 60 + 50 = 155, 200 − 155 = 45. 5) 60 to 90 is a change of 30; 120 to 95 is a change of 25. A change can go up or down: we compare the SIZE of the change.

p4l9-explore1.note: Minutes 8 to 13. Pairs plot the queue on a blank grid (online: printed grid or squared paper on camera). Ask them to predict first: when is the queue longest? Let pairs choose their own scale: lines worth 1, 2 or 5 all work if the lines are equal steps; a scale of 1 needs 22 lines. Hint for anyone unsure: try 2 per line (the biggest number is 22, so 12 lines are enough). Go further (on the slide), for any child who wants it: between which two times did the queue grow the most? Can you see it without working out every change? GO FURTHER (on the slide from minute 8, so nobody waits): Draw the same graph again with a different scale. Does the story look different? Why? Answer: Yes. A scale with small steps, or one that starts above 0, makes the line look steeper; big steps make it look flatter. The numbers are the same: only the picture changed.

p4l9-explore2.note: Minutes 13 to 18. Gather pairs and compare graphs: are the shapes the same even if the scales are different? (Yes, if the steps are equal.) Answers: 1) 12:30, with 22 people. 2) 11:30 to 12:00: up 9 (the steepest line going up; the changes are up 5, up 9, up 4, down 7, down 8, down 4). 3) 2:00 (3 people) or 11:00 (4 people): the shortest queues. Do NOT teach the steepest-line idea yet if nobody notices it: the next slides teach it.

p4l9-teach1.note: Teach. Click through the steps, then the red and teal reading lines. Think-aloud: "First the title and the axes, so I know what is counted and when. Then the scale: 0, 10, 20 on the numbered lines, so each numbered line is worth 10, and the faint line between is 5. Tuesday's point sits on the 40 line. Monday's point is halfway between 20 and 30: 25." Ask children to read Wednesday (35), Thursday (60) and Friday (50) on whiteboards. Common mistake: reading each line as 1.

p4l9-we1.note: Click to list each change, then the highlight, the answer and the rule. Think-aloud: "I list the change between each pair of neighbours and write up or down. The biggest increase is 25, Wednesday to Thursday. Look: on the graph it is the steepest line going up. So I can spot the biggest change by looking, then check it by working out." Ask: "Which is the biggest DEcrease?" (Thursday to Friday, 10). Worksheet Q1 asks for both.

p4l9-try1.note: Whiteboards, then click. a) 25 + 40 + 35 + 60 + 50 = 210 (make 100s: 40 + 60 and 25 + 35 + 50 = 110). b) Thursday to Friday, down 10 (Tuesday to Wednesday is only down 5). c) 60 − 25 = 35. Watch for children who answer b) with "Friday" only: a change is BETWEEN two days.

p4l9-we2.note: Click: each step, then its row fills in. Think-aloud: "A row must add up to its total. Ali has 26 and a missing number, total 61: 61 − 26 = 35. Then Mei. Ravi's total is the two numbers added. Last, I add down the columns. Then the best part: the check. The column totals and the row totals must both make the same grand total, 178. If they do not, I have made a mistake somewhere." Worksheet Q2 is the same kind of table.

p4l9-try2.note: Whiteboards. a) 30 + 45 + 35 = 110, 150 − 110 = 40. b) 60 − 28 = 32. c) 90 shared equally: 45 and 45. Check each by adding back up to the total.

p4l9-key.note: Say the key idea together. Common mistakes to watch for during the worksheet: (1) Reading the scale as 1 for each line when each line is worth 10 (or 5), so 75 is read as 7 and a half. (2) Looking only for the biggest increase and missing a bigger decrease, or comparing the heights of points instead of the change between them. (3) Comparing two graphs by how steep the lines look without checking where each scale starts and what each line is worth.

p4l9-break.note: Four minutes. Stories to call: a slow climb then flat; a fast drop; up, up, up then a crash; flat, then a sudden jump. Online: children stay in view of the camera and move in place.

p4l9-ws1.note: Minutes 34 to 50. Walk around. Ask "What is one line worth?" and "How can you check?" before giving any help. Q1d asks for a reason from the story: the stall is next to an office. CHOOSING: after question 3 every child may carry on or try the Think harder page. Invite the WHOLE group ("when you have finished Start here you can choose Think harder, Go further or the Investigation"); never message a child privately, never name a child, never announce who is on which page. If one child of a pair wants to move on, do not split the pair unless both agree; if a pair does lose a member, join the other child to another pair or to yourself straight away. Children on Think harder keep working through the page check; reading along is optional.

p4l9-ws1ans.note: Click each answer after a pair explains. Q1: the changes are up 15, down 5, up 25, down 10, down 40, up 5. Saturday and Sunday: 25 + 30 = 55. Q2: 85 − 38 = 47, 70 − 29 = 41, 45 + 52 = 97; check 124 + 128 = 252 = 85 + 70 + 97. b) Week 3 is 6 more for each of the 3 classes: 128 + 18 = 146.

p4l9-teachtwo.note: Teach before worksheet page 2 (Q3 has two lines). Use the key (legend) first: "Which line is which?" Click the steps. Think-aloud: "Q starts taller, but P grows faster: its line is steeper. Every week P catches up by 2 cm. The gap was 6, then 4, then 2, then 0: they cross at week 4. After that P is taller." Your turn: 20 − 18 = 2 cm. Do not do Q3 for them: Ali and Mei have different numbers.

p4l9-teachsteps.note: Teach before worksheet page 2 (Q4, Siti's pages). Ask first: "How many jumps from Day 1 to Day 4?" Many children say 4. Count the gaps on the graph: 1 to 2, 2 to 3, 3 to 4: 3 jumps. Click the steps, then the full line appears. Check: 8, 12, 16, 20, 24 all go up by 4. Total: 8 + 12 + 16 + 20 + 24 = 80 (or 5 days × the middle day, 16).

p4l9-teachscale.note: Teach before worksheet page 2 (Q5, the two shops). Ask first: "Which car park got much busier?" Most children say Graph 2. Then let them read the numbers from both graphs: they are the same! Click. Think-aloud: "Graph 2 does not start at 0. It starts at 50, and each line is only 2, so a small change looks huge. Graph 1 starts at 0, so the same change looks tiny. Neither graph is wrong, but Graph 2 can trick you." Ask: "Who might want to draw Graph 2? Why?" (someone who wants the change to look big, like an advert).

p4l9-ws2.note: Children work alone. Note who still reads every line as 1, and who compares the graphs by their look only. SOLO PAGE CAP: Page 2 is on your own. Aim for Q3 and Q4 first. Q5 is a choice for the last few minutes. Children who finish choose Think harder, Go further or the Investigation; nobody is told which.

p4l9-ws2ans.note: Click after a child explains. Q3: Ali goes up $10 a week, Mei $5; the gap of $20 in week 1 closes by $5 each week, so they meet in week 5 ($50) and Ali is ahead from week 6. Week 8: Ali 80, Mei 65. Q4: Day 2 to Day 5 is 3 jumps, 26 − 14 = 12, 12 ÷ 3 = 4; total 10 + 14 + 18 + 22 + 26 = 90. Q5: A goes 20 to 80, B goes 44 to 56. The lines look the same because each graph was stretched to fit its own scale.

p4l9-stretch.note: Answers (same four questions as the printed Think harder page): 1) Neither: both have 34 girls. (4A: 28 + 6 = 34. 4B: 63 − 5 = 58, 58 ÷ 2 = 29 boys, 29 + 5 = 34 girls.) 2) Ali 175 and Mei 275, so Mei has 100 more. She is not right: double Ali's is 350, and 275 is less than that. (Her point is more than twice as many lines up, 7 against 3, but the scale starts at 100, so counting lines gives the wrong picture.) 3) Monday 40, Tuesday 55, Wednesday 70, Thursday 55, Friday 40. Friday: 40 cups. Thursday (55) matches Tuesday (55). 4) From age 7 to 8 (7 cm). Altogether 17 cm.

p4l9-challenge.note: Pairs try first, then use the "see it" slide if stuck, then the walk-through. These are Go further Q5 and Q6. Answers: 1) A 34, B 17, C 27, D 22. 2) After 4 hours: 56 litres each.

p4l9-chdiag.note: Show after pairs have tried Go further, or if they are stuck. The pictures show the problem, not the answer. Ask: In Q1, how many equal bars can you see if you take away the 10 and the 22? In Q2, what happens to the GAP between the tanks every hour? Answers are in the Go further slide notes.

p4l9-chwalk.note: Use after pairs have tried. Q1: the bar model turns "twice as many" and "10 more" into equal bars; check 34 + 17 + 27 + 22 = 100. Q2: a table works (keep going hour by hour), but the gap idea is quicker: Tank A goes down and Tank B goes up, so the gap shrinks by both amounts each hour. On a line graph the two lines cross at hour 4, at 56 litres. After that, Tank B has more.

p4l9-talk.note: Minutes 80 to 85. Pairs talk for 2 minutes, then share. Answer: the scales are different. If a scale starts at a big number, or each line is worth very little, a small change looks huge. To compare fairly, use the same scale for both graphs, starting at 0. Second question if time: "Why did we list the changes instead of just looking at the highest point?" (the highest point shows the biggest number, not the biggest change). Praise the reasons, not only the answers. TALK TIME RULES: ask for volunteers first; a child may always pass; never call on a child by name to answer; no public tallies, scores or rankings; praise the reason, not the child. If a question uses a mistaken idea (a character who gets it wrong), present it as the character's idea and ask "What would you say to them?" so no child owns the mistake.

p4l9-exit.note: Minutes 85 to 88. Answer: Tuesday to Wednesday, a decrease of 30 (the other changes are up 15 and up 25). Watch for children who choose Wednesday to Thursday (the biggest INCREASE, 25). Extension: draw two line graphs of 52, 54, 56, 58, one that makes the change look huge and one that makes it look tiny.

p4l9-reflect.note: Minutes 88 to 90 (2 minutes). LOOKING BACK. Children fill in the box on the Investigation page, the page every child has (something I did well; the hardest part was; what helped me; one thing I could try next). Say: "You can write, tick or pass. Ticking I am still stuck is a good thing to do: it tells me where to help." Model one yourself first: "Something I did well: I read the scale first. The hardest part was reading between the lines on the scale. What helped me: writing what each line was worth. One thing I could try next: writing the scale before I read any numbers." Do not ask anyone to read theirs out. If a child wants to share, take one volunteer and thank them for the strategy. Never grade it, never correct it, never collect it for marks and never show it to the group. You may look at a child's page only when the child holds it to your camera. Never ask for photos or private messages. If I am still stuck is ticked, check in during the open session: a quick visit to the shared breakout room or a hand signal, with a parent nearby. Never send a DM. Praise strategies ("you drew it", "you asked for help"), not speed or scores.
